blocks.text: Given a string s, return the longest substring of it that reads the same forward and backward.

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding the Longest Mirror Image Inside a Sentence
blocks.text: Like scanning a long word or phrase for the longest stretch that reads identically whether read left to right or right to left, the same way a name like "racecar" mirrors perfectly around its middle letter.

blocks.caption: Find the longest stretch of characters that reads the same in both directions

blocks.text: A single character is trivially its own palindrome, so the answer is simply "a".
It helps to ask what actually defines a palindrome structurally, rather than treating every substring as an independent guess to verify.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The brute force checks every substring directly with a two pointer palindrome test, the same symmetric comparison used in Valid Palindrome, but it repeats this check across a huge number of overlapping candidate substrings independently.

Observation 2: Every palindrome is uniquely defined by its own center, either a single character for an odd length palindrome, or the gap between two characters for an even length one, so instead of picking two ends and checking inward, a center can be picked and expansion can happen outward.

Observation 3: Trying every one of the 2n minus 1 possible centers and expanding each one outward only as far as both sides genuinely keep matching finds the true longest palindrome directly, with no separate substring extraction and verification step at all.

Observation 4: Repeated Substring Pattern already showed that reusing previously learned structural information, instead of recomputing it from scratch, can drop a problem's complexity further; Manacher's algorithm applies that same idea here, reusing an already known mirrored radius whenever the current center falls inside a previously found palindrome, confirmed by tracing s equal to "babad" through the full algorithm to the correct answer, "bab".
Recognizing that a palindrome is defined by its center, not its two ends, is what replaces verifying every substring independently with expanding outward from every possible center.
Check every possible substring directly, verify whether each one is a palindrome, and keep track of the longest one found.

items: For every starting index i and every ending index j at or after i, extract the substring from i to j.
Check whether that substring reads the same forward and backward.
Keep the longest substring found that passes the check.

codes.python:
def longest_palindrome(s):
    n = len(s)
    best = ""
    for i in range(n):                                      # every possible starting index
        for j in range(i, n):                                  # every possible ending index
            candidate = s[i:j + 1]
            if candidate == candidate[::-1] and len(candidate) > len(best):
                best = candidate                                    # verify it is a palindrome directly
    return best


if __name__ == "__main__":
    s = "babad"
    print(longest_palindrome(s))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every possible pair of start and end indices is tried, so every possible substring of s is considered exactly once.
Each candidate is verified using the same two pointer, converge from both ends, palindrome check used in Valid Palindrome.
Only a longer valid palindrome ever replaces the current best, so the running best always reflects the longest one confirmed so far.

blocks.text: Every possible substring is directly checked, so the true longest palindrome is guaranteed to be found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n cubed), for O(n squared) substrings, each taking up to O(n) to verify.
Space: O(n), for the substrings being built and checked.

Limitation: most substrings are checked completely independently, even though palindromes have a useful structural property: a longer palindrome always contains a shorter palindrome at its exact center.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the brute force works but is wasteful: it builds and verifies an enormous number of overlapping substrings independently, throwing away the fact that palindromes are naturally centered.

What expanding from a center fixes directly: starting at a single potential center and growing outward only while both sides genuinely match finds the exact widest palindrome at that center, with no wasted verification of substrings that could never be maximal.

What has to be covered to catch every case: both single character centers, for odd length palindromes, and the gaps between characters, for even length ones, since a palindrome can center on either.

The core idea: try all 2n minus 1 possible centers, expand each outward while matching, and keep the widest successful expansion found across all of them.

Every palindrome has a center, either a single character (for odd length palindromes) or a gap between two characters (for even length palindromes). For each of the 2n minus 1 possible centers, expand outward one step at a time in both directions simultaneously, as long as the characters on both sides keep matching. The widest successful expansion at any center gives the longest palindrome centered there, and the best across all centers is the overall answer.
Try every possible center and expand outward while both sides match.
Dry run for s = "babad", center at index 1 (the "a")

blocks.caption: Optimized: expand outward from every possible center, single character and between character

blocks.text: This works because expanding outward from a center only continues while the characters on both sides genuinely match, so the moment expansion stops, the widest palindrome centered there has been found exactly, and repeating this for every possible center guarantees the true longest palindrome anywhere in the string is discovered.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), since each of the 2n minus 1 centers can expand up to O(n) times.
Space: O(1) extra, not counting the answer substring.

The expand around center approach still redoes work whenever two overlapping palindromes exist. Manacher's algorithm processes every center in a single left to right pass, and whenever the current center falls inside a previously found palindrome, it reuses the already known radius of the mirrored position on the other side of that palindrome's center as a starting point, only expanding further when genuinely necessary. This brings the total work for all centers combined down to linear time.

blocks.caption: Further optimization: reuse previously computed radius information from mirrored centers

codes.python:
def longest_palindrome(s):
    if not s:
        return ""
    transformed = "#" + "#".join(s) + "#"                    # insert separators so every palindrome has odd length
    n = len(transformed)
    radius = [0] * n
    center = right = 0
    for i in range(n):
        if i < right:
            mirror = 2 * center - i
            radius[i] = min(right - i, radius[mirror])           # reuse the mirrored center's known radius
        while i - radius[i] - 1 >= 0 and i + radius[i] + 1 < n and \
                transformed[i - radius[i] - 1] == transformed[i + radius[i] + 1]:
            radius[i] += 1                                         # only expand further if genuinely needed
        if i + radius[i] > right:
            center, right = i, i + radius[i]
    max_radius = max(radius)
    center_index = radius.index(max_radius)
    start = (center_index - max_radius) // 2
    return s[start:start + max_radius]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    s = "babad"
    print(longest_palindrome(s))

items: Separator characters are inserted between every pair of original characters so that every palindrome, odd or even length in the original string, becomes an odd length palindrome in the transformed string, unifying both cases into one procedure.

When the current position falls within the rightmost boundary of a previously discovered palindrome, its mirrored position's already known radius gives a safe starting radius, since the two sides of that outer palindrome must mirror each other.
Expansion only continues past that reused starting radius when genuinely necessary, and the outer boundary is updated whenever a new palindrome extends further right than any found so far.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), every position's expansion work is bounded by the total growth of the rightmost known palindrome boundary across the whole pass.
Space: O(n), for the transformed string and the radius array.

blocks.text: The expand around center approach is usually sufficient and much easier to implement correctly under interview pressure, while Manacher's algorithm is the specialized linear time technique worth mentioning when asked to optimize further, since it exploits the mirror symmetry inherent to palindromes.

items: Forgetting to check both odd length centers (single character) and even length centers (between two characters), which misses valid even length palindromes entirely.
Recomputing a palindrome check on an already built substring instead of expanding directly on the original string, which wastes memory building many intermediate substrings.

blocks.text: Present the expand around center approach first, since it is intuitive and sufficient for most interviews, then mention Manacher's algorithm by name as the further optimization if explicitly asked to do better than O(n squared).

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid checking every substring", think: expand outward from every possible center instead.
If the interviewer says "can you do better than O(n squared)", think: Manacher's algorithm, reusing mirrored radius information in a single linear pass.
If the interviewer says "how do you handle even length palindromes", think: expand from a center placed between two characters, not just from single characters.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force: O(n cubed) time, O(n) space. Optimized (expand around center): O(n squared) time, O(1) extra space. Further optimized (Manacher's algorithm): O(n) time, O(n) space.

items: Pattern: expand outward from every possible center, further optimized with Manacher's algorithm reusing mirrored radius information.

Core Idea: every palindrome is defined by its own center, so trying all 2n minus 1 centers and expanding outward while matching finds the answer directly, and reusing mirrored radius information reduces this further to linear time.
Time: O(n cubed) for the brute force, O(n squared) for expand around center, O(n) for Manacher's algorithm.
Space: O(n) for the brute force, O(1) extra for expand around center, O(n) for Manacher's algorithm.

Most Important Observation: a palindrome's center, not its endpoints, is the natural anchor to search from, and mirror symmetry around a known palindrome's center lets already computed information be reused instead of recomputed.
Interview Difficulty: expand around center is standard and expected; Manacher's algorithm is advanced and worth naming, but rarely required to implement from memory under time pressure.
One line memory trick: expand outward from every center, both single character and between character, and keep the widest match.
